
## 1. Load the processed data

```{r load}
# Open the project's .Rproj file before running chunks.
# Install psych once in the Console if needed: install.packages("psych")
install.packages("psych")
library(psych)

h1Data <- read.csv("h data/processed_data/221A_h1.csv")
h2Data <- read.csv("h data/processed_data/221A_h2.csv")


```

## 2. Look at the distribution first

```{r histogram}
# A histogram groups numerical values into intervals (bins).
# Bar height shows how many observations fall in each interval.
# Start by looking at the distribution before calculating summary statistics.
hist(h1Data$viewtotal)
hist(h2Data$Time_social_media_1)
hist(h2Data$attracttotal)

# Add readable labels to the same histogram.
hist(h1Data$viewtotal,
     main="Distribution of Traditional Gender Beliefs",
     xlab="Composite Score of Traditional Gender Beliefs 
     (Lower score is less traditional)")

hist(h2Data$attracttotal,
     main="Distribution of Belief in Importance of Attractiveness",
     xlab="Composite Score")

hist(h2Data$Time_social_media_1,
     main="Distribution of Social Media Usage",
     xlab="Minutes of Social Media Use Per Week")

```

## 3. One statistic at a time

```{r individual_statistics}
# Mean: add the scores and divide by the number of observed responses.
mean(h2Data$attracttotal, na.rm=TRUE)
mean(h2Data$Time_social_media_1, na.rm=TRUE)
mean(h1Data$viewtotal, na.rm=TRUE)

# Median: the middle score after sorting the responses.
median(h2Data$attracttotal, na.rm=TRUE)
median(h2Data$Time_social_media_1, na.rm=TRUE)
median(h1Data$viewtotal, na.rm=TRUE)

# Table: count how many people are in each category.
# Table is best for categorical variables
table(h2Data$attracttotal, useNA= "ifany")
table(h2Data$Time_social_media_1, useNA= "ifany")
table(h1Data$viewtotal, useNA = "ifany")

# Range: return the minimum and maximum, rather than their difference.
range(h2Data$attracttotal, na.rm=TRUE)
range(h2Data$Time_social_media_1, na.rm=TRUE)
range(h1Data$viewtotal, na.rm=TRUE)


# IQR: the 75th percentile minus the 25th percentile.
#large value means data is spread out, low number means data is dense
IQR(h2Data$attracttotal, na.rm=TRUE)
IQR(h2Data$Time_social_media_1, na.rm=TRUE)
IQR(h1Data$viewtotal, na.rm=TRUE)

```

## 4. Standardize a variable

```{r standardize}
# scale() uses z = (original score - mean) / standard deviation by default.
# Keep the original commitment scores and store the standardized values separately.
# scale() returns a matrix; as.numeric() makes a simple numeric column.
(h2Data$attracttotal - mean(h2Data$attracttotal, na.rm=TRUE))/sd(h2Data$attracttotal, na.rm=TRUE)
(h2Data$Time_social_media_1 - mean(h2Data$Time_social_media_1, na.rm=TRUE))/sd(h2Data$Time_social_media_1, na.rm=TRUE)
(h1Data$viewtotal - mean(h1Data$viewtotal, na.rm=TRUE))/sd(h1Data$viewtotal, na.rm=TRUE)

#will return a vector of z-scores
h2Data$attracttotal_z <- scale(h2Data$attracttotal)
h2Data$Time_social_media_z <- scale(h2Data$Time_social_media_1)
h1Data$viewtotal_z <- scale(h1Data$viewtotal)


# Standardized scores have mean approximately 0 and standard deviation 1. (SANITY CHECK)
mean(h2Data$attracttotal_z, na.rm=TRUE) 
sd(h2Data$attracttotal_z, na.rm=TRUE)

mean(h2Data$Time_social_media_z, na.rm=TRUE) 
sd(h2Data$Time_social_media_z, na.rm=TRUE)

mean(h1Data$viewtotal_z, na.rm=TRUE) 
sd(h1Data$viewtotal_z, na.rm=TRUE)

```

## 5. Covariance and correlation

```{r association}
# Covariance describes whether two variables tend to move together.
# Positive: higher values tend to occur together. Negative: higher values tend to accompany lower values.
# Its size depends on the units and is not restricted to -1 through 1.
cov(h2Data$Time_social_media_1, h2Data$attracttotal, use ="complete.obs")

# Pearson correlation expresses a linear association on a -1 to 1 scale.
cor(h2Data$Time_social_media_1, h2Data$attracttotal, use ="complete.obs")

# Select numerical variables only; do not include participant IDs or category codes. 
corData <- h2Data[,c("Time_social_media_1","attracttotal")]

# A correlation matrix gives the correlation for each pair of columns.
# The diagonal is 1 because each variable is correlated with itself.
cor(corData, use="complete.obs")

```

## 6. Several statistics at once

```{r combined_summaries}
# summary() reports minimum, quartiles, median, mean, maximum, and missing counts when present.
summary(corData)

# psych::describe() reports n, mean, SD, median, minimum, maximum, range width (max minus min), skewness, kurtosis, and other summaries.
psych::describe(corData)

# However it does not report every statistic above: compute IQR, cov(), and cor() separately.
IQR(h2Data$attracttotal, na.rm=TRUE, type=7)

IQR(h2Data$Time_social_media_1, na.rm=TRUE, type=7)

IQR(h1Data$viewtotal, na.rm=TRUE, type=7)





```
